stops.name: The Cluses of Susa, the Lombard wall turned
stops.campa: Desiderius waits behind the ancient walls of the cluses, the fortified throat of the Susa valley, and the passes are barred. Then a Frankish detachment finds a path over the bare ridges (the canon remembers a nameless Lombard jongleur who sang the way, and later legend a mountain guide) and comes down behind the barrier. The Lombards wake to Franks above and Franks before them, abandon the works in a night without a battle, and stream back onto the plain. The gate of Italy stands open. Charles rides through the broken cluses under the October snow-light.

stops.name: Pavia, the siege of the Lombard capital begins
stops.campa: Desiderius shuts himself in Pavia, the brick-walled capital of the Lombards on the Ticino, and Charles, refusing the cost of a storm, sits down to starve it. He sends for Hildegard the queen and his children to winter with him before the walls: the siege will be a royal court in canvas. Adelchis the king's son has fled to Verona with Carloman's widow and her boys, the last loose threads of the Frankish succession, gathered conveniently under one distant roof. The rains come; the Franks build huts; Pavia begins its slow year of hunger.

stops.name: Verona, the widow's sons taken
stops.campa: Leaving the siege lines, Charles marches on Verona, strongest of Lombard cities. It does not test him: Gerberga, Carloman's widow, comes out with her sons and gives herself into the hands of the brother-in-law she fled. Adelchis slips away east to end his days a Byzantine patrician, an exile with a title and no country. The canon then closes over the little princes: they pass from the record without a word, absorbed into the king's mercy or his silence. Charles returns to the siege with the last rival Carolingian blood riding in his baggage.

stops.name: Rome, Saint Peter's, Easter: the king climbs the steps on his knees
stops.campa: Leaving the siege at Pavia, Charles rides south and on Holy Saturday sees Rome for the first time in his life. Pope Hadrian, taken by surprise, sends the banners of the city thirty miles up the road; the militia and the schools of the foreigners meet him with palms and crosses, singing. At the steps of Saint Peter's the king of the Franks dismounts and goes up on his knees, kissing each stair one by one, until at the top Hadrian waits and the two men embrace. Easter falls the next day. Within the week Charles renews on the apostle's body his father's donation to Peter.
stops.quote: He kissed every single step one by one as he climbed up to the pontiff.
stops.quote_source: Liber Pontificalis, Life of Hadrian I

stops.name: Pavia falls: the Iron Crown of the Lombards
stops.campa: In June, after nine months, plague and famine open the gates of Pavia. Desiderius is taken with his treasure and sent north to a monastery, to end as a monk the line of Alboin. Charles does what no Frank has done: he does not annex, he assumes; from this day he signs himself king of the Franks AND of the Lombards. The tradition sets on his head the Iron Crown, the golden circlet closed with a slim band of iron beaten from a nail of the True Cross, so that whoever wears Lombardy wears the Passion itself. One king now, both sides of the Alps.

stops.name: Paderborn, the Saracens of Zaragoza kneel at the Saxon assembly
stops.campa: Charles holds the great assembly for the first time inside Saxony, at Paderborn by the two hundred springs of the Pader, as if the conquest were finished. And into this camp of baptisms rides the unforeseen: Sulayman al-Arabi, governor of Barcelona, with envoys of Zaragoza, offering their cities to the king of the Franks against the emir of Cordoba. The map of the world tilts. Charles, fresh from felling one paganism, hears Spain offered like fruit. Only Widukind is absent from the oath-taking, fled to the Danes: the one empty place at the feast, and the costly one.

stops.name: Chasseneuil, the queen left behind; Louis born
stops.campa: The host masses for Spain, and at the villa of Chasseneuil in Aquitaine the king leaves Hildegard, great with child. While he is beyond the Pyrenees she is delivered of twin boys; one dies, and the one who lives is named Louis: Hlodowig, Clovis's own name reborn in the family that replaced his line. The canon likes the arithmetic: as Roland dies in the pass, the future emperor is in his cradle. Louis the Pious, who will inherit everything, is born into the very summer of the great defeat.

stops.name: Pamplona, the gates opened
stops.campa: Charles crosses the western passes with half the host (the other half swings through Septimania toward the Ebro), and Pamplona, city of the Basques under Saracen lordship, opens its gates to him. It is smooth, too smooth; the mountain people watch the Frankish column from the ridgelines and say nothing. The two armies are to meet at Zaragoza, where Sulayman's promise waits to be kept. The king rides through Navarre in early summer, the first Christian king in the peninsula since the Goths fell, sure that God is leading him as He led at Pavia.

stops.name: Zaragoza, the promised city refuses
stops.campa: Before the walls of Zaragoza the promise dies. Husayn, master of the city, shuts the gates: he made no oath, and the white walls above the Ebro stay silent against the whole Frankish host. There will be no second Pavia; a siege here, a thousand miles from the Rhine, with Saxony smoking behind him, is impossible, and Charles knows it. He takes hostages and gold, takes Sulayman himself in chains for a broken bargain, and turns the army around. In the Chanson this is where Ganelon's embassy plants treason; in the annals it is simply the turning: the first great enterprise that fails.

stops.name: Pamplona, the walls razed on the way home
stops.campa: Marching home, Charles stops at Pamplona and throws down its walls to the ground, that it may never rebel, a punishment laid on a city that had opened to him, and the Basques of the mountains watch this too. The revised annals say it plainly: Pampelona destructa. The army turns north into the defiles with its hostages, its wagons of Spanish gold, and, riding with the rear-guard, the prefect of the Breton march, Hruodland, whom the singers will make the nephew of the king. The mountains close over the road like water.

stops.name: The Pass of Ibaneta, Roncevaux: the rear-guard set
stops.campa: The fifteenth of August. The host files over the pass of Cize in a column stretched thin by the narrow ground, thick woods on either hand. The baggage and the rear-guard come last, and the canon sets the flower of the palace there: Eggihard master of the table, Anselm count of the palace, Roland of the Breton march; in the Chanson, the Twelve Peers with him and Ganelon's treason already sold to King Marsile. On the heights above Ibaneta the Basques lie in the timber, light-armed, patient, native to the dark of the woods. The main army passes down into Gascony, out of earshot. The trap holds its breath.
stops.quote: Eggihard, the King's steward; Anselm, Count Palatine; and Roland, Governor of the March of Brittany, with very many others, fell in this engagement.

stops.name: Roncevaux, Roland refuses the horn
stops.campa: The heathen host pours down the slopes, a hundred thousand in the song, and Oliver climbs a pine and sees the valley bright with hauberks. Three times he begs Roland: sound the oliphant, Charles will hear and turn the army. Three times Roland refuses. He will not shame his kin, will not have sweet France lowered for his sake. Oliver is wise, says the song, and Roland is brave, and the refusal is both the sin and the glory of France. The rear-guard draws Durendal and turns to face the whole of Spain.
stops.quote: Respunt Rollant: 'Jo fereie que fols! / En dulce France en perdreie mun los.'
